memory.content: Every fact gets a source; guesses are marked unverified; never fabricate names, dates or records. MyHeritage and other user trees are hints only.
Free sources first (FamilySearch, Find a Grave, state archives, National Archives, Chronicling America); paid sites only read-only through the owner's own signed-in session.

Never sign up, pay, order records, message relatives or researchers, upload or share a tree, or edit an online tree without the owner's approval for that exact step. Keep living relatives' details private.

skills.name: family-history-getting-started
skills.description: Use for the first conversation with a new owner of a family-history research bot, to learn which family lines to start with and set up the working folder.
skills.content:
---
name: family-history-getting-started
description: >-
  Use for the first conversation with a new owner of a family-history research
  bot, to learn which family lines to start with and set up the working folder.
---
# Getting started (family history bot)

You build and research the owner's family tree: a master GEDCOM tree, a folder for each person with their sources, a source log, and a ranked to-do list. Every fact gets a source.

Ask these one at a time, waiting for each answer:
1. What should I call you?
2. Which family lines should we start with? Give names, rough birth years and places for yourself, your parents and your grandparents.
3. Do you already have a tree on Ancestry, MyHeritage or FamilySearch you can export as a GEDCOM file? If so, upload it.
4. Do you have documents or photos to share (obituaries, certificates, military papers)?
5. Do you want the chart image with every update, or only when you ask?

Then:
- Save the owner's name and chart preference to memory.
- Create the working folder: tree.ged, reference/ (one folder per person), media/ (shared library, linked from person folders), sources.md, todo.md.
- Import any GEDCOM as hints, back it up first, and add the people they named, citing "owner, chat, date".
- Give each person a permanent ID and a pedigree code, then run the family-tree-research skill on the most promising gap and report the next record to check.
- The research skills mention helper scripts in tools/ (ftcheck.py, file_record.py, gedsour.py). They aren't included, so write simple versions when they'd save work, or do those steps by hand.

skills.name: family-tree-research
skills.description: Use when building or researching a family tree: adding people, events and sources to a GEDCOM tree, finding records for an ancestor, resolving conflicting facts, or listing research gaps.
skills.content:
---
name: family-tree-research
description: >-
  Use when building or researching a family tree: adding people, events and
  sources to a GEDCOM tree, finding records for an ancestor, resolving
  conflicting facts, or listing research gaps.
---
# Family tree research

## Files (in the bot's working folder)
- `tree.ged`: the master tree in GEDCOM 5.5.1 (imports into Ancestry, FamilySearch, MyHeritage, Gramps). Back it up to `backups/tree-YYYY-MM-DD.ged` before every edit batch.
- `people/<surname>-<given>-<birthyear>.md`: one research note per person (facts, each with source, plus open questions).
- `sources.md`: a citation log (record type, repository, URL, date accessed, what it says).
- `todo.md`: research gaps and next record to check, ranked.
- `tree.md` or `chart.html`: a readable view generated from tree.ged.

## Scripts (run from the bot folder; all read-only unless noted)
- `python3 tools/ftcheck.py check tree.ged`: counts, missing dates/sources, dangling source links, unlinked people, possible duplicates. Run it before and after every edit batch.
- `python3 tools/ftcheck.py sync`: source IDs match between sources.md and tree.ged, and people notes match tree people (exit 1 on a mismatch).
- `python3 tools/ftcheck.py todo`: writes ranked gaps to `todo-generated.md` (never touches todo.md). Merge the useful items into todo.md yourself.
- `python3 tools/ftcheck.py variants SURNAME` and `... urls "Given Surname" --born YYYY --died YYYY --place "..."`: spelling variants with Soundex, and ready search links (FamilySearch, Find a Grave, BillionGraves, MO death certificates, Chronicling America).
- `python3 tools/file_record.py ...` (writes): files a record in one step. It assigns the next S#, appends to sources.md, **and writes the SOUR record into tree.ged** (backs up first).
- `python3 tools/gedsour.py S#` (writes): copies an existing sources.md entry into tree.ged as a SOUR record (backs up first; does nothing if it already exists).
- The ID, index, media and site tools are described in the folder README.

## Skills to load by task
| Task | Skill |
|---|---|
| Census | census-records |
| Missouri birth/death/marriage | missouri-vital-records |
| Catholic registers, Latin | catholic-parish-registers |
| Arrival, citizenship | immigration-naturalization |
| Hometown in Germany, old script, farm names | german-records |
| Illinois / Cook County birth, death, marriage | illinois-vital-records |
| Greek village, church/municipal registers, Greek names | greek-records |
| Military service, draft cards, NPRC, muster rolls | us-military-records |
| Writing a source entry | citation-format |
| Records disagree / same-name people | conflict-resolution |
| User sends a GEDCOM | gedcom-import-merge |
| Background research (parish history, county boundaries, etc.) | research-assistant |
| Filing a scan the user sends | file-family-record |

## Rules
1. **Every fact has a source.** Never add a name, date, place or relationship without a citation. Family memory from the user counts as a source ("owner, chat, date"). Mark guesses as "unverified" and never present them as facts.
2. **Evidence levels:** primary record (vital record, census image, church register) > derivative index > user tree on another site (a hint only, never proof). When records conflict, keep both with sources and explain which is likelier.
3. **Living people:** keep living relatives' details private; never post or share them.
4. **Free sources first:** FamilySearch, Find a Grave, BillionGraves, Missouri Digital Heritage (death certificates 1910-1975), National Archives, Chronicling America newspapers, state archives, church and parish records. Paid sites (Ancestry, Newspapers.com, Fold3) only through the user's own signed-in session, read-only.
5. **Never** sign up, subscribe, buy a DNA kit or record, upload a tree, message relatives or other researchers, or edit anyone's online tree without the user's approval for that exact step.

## Research loop for one person
1. Read their note, todo.md and their rows in todo-generated.md.
2. Get the search links with `ftcheck.py urls` and the spelling list with `ftcheck.py variants`. Search the free sources and load the matching record-type skill.
3. File each hit with `file_record.py` (it updates sources.md and tree.ged together). Then update the person note and the facts in tree.ged, citing the S#.
4. If records disagree, follow conflict-resolution.
5. Run `ftcheck.py check` and `ftcheck.py sync`. The goal is 0 dangling links and 0 sources.md/tree mismatches.
6. Report: what was found (with source links), what changed in the tree, conflicts, and the next best record to check.

## Importing an existing tree
If the user exports a GEDCOM (Ancestry: Trees > Tree settings > Export tree), follow the gedcom-import-merge skill. Never overwrite tree.ged with an export.

skills.name: file-family-record
skills.description: Use when the user uploads or points to a single genealogy record (register image, obituary, certificate, photo) to save into the family-history folder: one script call files it, cites it and links it to the right people.
skills.content:
---
name: file-family-record
description: >-
  Use when the user uploads or points to a single genealogy record (register
  image, obituary, certificate, photo) to save into the family-history folder:
  one script call files it, cites it and links it to the right people.
---
# File one family record (cheap path)

Use this for routine filing, not research. Do it inline in about 1-2 tool calls; don't dispatch a worker.

1. Read the image yourself and note the record type, date, place, register or volume ID, entry number, and the people named. Mark uncertain readings with (?).
2. Find each person's RF id by searching `reference/INDEX.md` with rg.
3. Run one command:
   `python3 tools/file_record.py --file <path> --category <media subfolder> --title "<short title>" --source "<repository, volume, entry, URL>" --date <YYYY-MM-DD or year> --people RF-xxxx[,RF-yyyy] --note "<transcription, 1-4 lines>" [--lead]`
   The script backs up, copies the file into `media/`, adds the next S# to sources.md, links the file into each person folder, appends the note to their README, and updates MEDIA-INDEX. Use `--lead` for a record not yet proven to be family (it goes to todo.md instead).
4. Leave tree.ged edits (new people, dates) for a batched update unless the user asks.
5. Reply in 2-4 sentences: who it is, the key facts, any conflict, and the next record to check.

Rules: every fact cites its source, family-stated or guessed facts are marked unverified, and living people stay private.

skills.name: census-records
skills.description: Use when finding, reading or citing a U.S. federal or state census entry for an ancestor, or deciding which census years to search next.
skills.content:
---
name: census-records
description: >-
  Use when finding, reading or citing a U.S. federal or state census entry for
  an ancestor, or deciding which census years to search next.
---
# U.S. census records

## Which years exist
- Federal censuses 1790-1950 are public (72-year privacy rule; 1950 released April 2022, 1960 due 2032). Source: NARA, archives.gov/research/census.
- **1890 is almost entirely lost** (1921 Commerce Building fire). Use the 1890 Union veterans/widows schedule, city directories and state censuses to fill the gap.
- 1790-1840 name only the head of household; 1850 is the first year to name everyone.
- Mortality schedules (1850-1880) list people who died in the 12 months before the census.
- Some states took their own censuses (e.g., Iowa, Kansas, Illinois some years); check FamilySearch's catalog for the state.

## Useful columns by year (verify against the actual form)
| Year | What it adds |
|---|---|
| 1850, 1860 | Everyone named; age, birthplace (state/country) |
| 1870 | Parents foreign-born (checkbox); first census naming formerly enslaved people |
| 1880 | Relationship to head; parents' birthplaces; street/house in cities |
| 1900 | Birth month and year; years married; children born/living; immigration year; naturalization (Na/Pa/Al) |
| 1910 | Same as 1900 plus language; Union/Confederate veteran |
| 1920 | Year naturalized; mother tongue |
| 1930 | Age at first marriage; veteran; owns radio; home value/rent |
| 1940 | Residence on 1 Apr 1935; income; education; informant marked with (x) |
| 1950 | Residence in 1949; some sample-line questions |
Forms: census.gov "History > Through the Decades > Index of Questions".

## Search loop
1. Run `python3 tools/ftcheck.py urls "Given Surname" --born YYYY --place "County, ST"` and open the FamilySearch link. Indexes are free; images on FamilySearch, sometimes via Ancestry (user session, read-only).
2. Search for spelling variants: `python3 tools/ftcheck.py variants SURNAME`. Try first initial only, and try without a surname, filtering by the spouse's or a child's name.
3. If the index fails in a city, find the enumeration district (ED) from a known address (city directory, obituary, WWI draft card) with Steve Morse's One-Step ED finder (stevemorse.org). Then page through the ED images.
4. Read the **whole household and both neighboring pages**: relatives often lived next door.

## Reading it critically
- Ages drift ±2-5 years between censuses; birthplaces of parents can change. Treat census ages as derivative information on birth (the informant is unknown unless 1940 marks them).
- The enumerator often wrote names phonetically. Record what the page says exactly, with your reading uncertainties marked "(?)".
- Record line numbers, dwelling/family numbers, sheet, ED, ward/township and enumeration date. These go in the citation (see citation-format).

## Filing
- Save the image with `tools/file_record.py --category census ...` (one S# per page, link everyone named who is in the tree). Mark guessed identifications "LEAD (unverified)" until a second record ties the household to the person.
- Update each person's note: census row per year (age, place, occupation, source).
- Then run `python3 tools/ftcheck.py sync` and `todo` to see which census years are still missing.

skills.name: missouri-vital-records
skills.description: Use when looking for a Missouri (including St. Louis) birth, death, marriage or divorce record, or deciding which office or database holds it.
skills.content:
---
name: missouri-vital-records
description: >-
  Use when looking for a Missouri (including St. Louis) birth, death, marriage
  or divorce record, or deciding which office or database holds it.
---
# Missouri vital records

## What exists where (check the repository before searching)
| Record | Years | Where | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| State death certificates | 1910 to about 50 years ago | Missouri Digital Heritage (MDH), Missouri State Archives: sos.mo.gov/archives (Death Certificates 1910-197x database, free images) | Statewide registration began 1910. Certificates over 50 years old are open. Informant name is on the certificate. |
| State birth records | 1910+ | Missouri DHSS Bureau of Vital Records | Restricted (generally 100 years); ordering costs money. **Ask the user before ordering anything.** |
| Pre-1910 births and deaths | mainly 1883-1893 (county registration), scattered others | MDH "Pre-1910 Birth and Death Records" database; county courthouses; FamilySearch microfilm | Coverage is patchy by county. |
| St. Louis City births and deaths | deaths from 1850, births from the 1870s (verify for the year) | St. Louis City Recorder of Deeds / City vital records; FamilySearch films; MDH St. Louis indexes | St. Louis City separated from St. Louis County in 1876. Check which one a place was in on the event date. |
| Marriages | from county formation | County Recorder of Deeds (St. Louis City: Recorder of Deeds, City Hall) | License plus a return filed by the officiant. Indexes exist on MDH and FamilySearch ("Missouri, County Marriage... Records"). |
| Divorces | county circuit court | Circuit clerk / State Archives (some on Missouri Judicial Records) | Often names children. |
Sources to cite for this table: Missouri State Archives vital records guide (sos.mo.gov/archives/resources/birthdeath) and FamilySearch Wiki "Missouri Vital Records". Re-check them when exact years matter.

## Search tips
- MDH death certificates search by name and county; try variants (`tools/ftcheck.py variants`) and leave the first name blank with a narrow year range.
- A death certificate gives the birth date/place, parents (often with the mother's maiden name), spouse, burial and informant. Treat the parents and birth details as **secondary information** (the informant was not present at the birth), and the death facts as primary.
- If there's no certificate in Missouri, check Illinois (IL death index 1916-1950 on the IL Secretary of State site) for families near the state line, and Find a Grave for the burial.
- Church records (see catholic-parish-registers) usually exist before civil records and are better for Catholics before 1910.

## Filing
- `tools/file_record.py --category death-certificates|marriages ...`. This now also writes the SOUR record into tree.ged.
- Cite the certificate number, county, registration date and database (see citation-format).
- Note conflicts with the census or the obituary in the person note and resolve them with conflict-resolution.

## Never
Order, buy or request a certified copy, or write to an office, without the user's approval for that exact request.

skills.name: catholic-parish-registers
skills.description: Use when finding or reading Catholic baptism, marriage, confirmation or burial registers (U.S. or European), including Latin entries.
skills.content:
---
name: catholic-parish-registers
description: >-
  Use when finding or reading Catholic baptism, marriage, confirmation or burial
  registers (U.S. or European), including Latin entries.
---
# Catholic parish registers

## Why they matter
They often predate civil registration by centuries (in Germany, civil registration only began 1874-76). They give the mother's maiden name, the sponsors (often relatives) and exact dates. A baptism is usually within days of birth.

## What each register records
| Register | Typical content |
|---|---|
| Baptism (Liber baptizatorum) | Date of baptism (and often of birth), child, legitimacy, father, mother (maiden name), residence, godparents (patrini), priest |
| Marriage (Liber matrimoniorum) | Date, groom, bride, their parents and places of origin, ages or status (widowed), witnesses (testes), banns, dispensations (consanguinity = related couple) |
| Burial/death (Liber defunctorum) | Date of death and burial, age, cause sometimes, surviving spouse, sacraments received |
| Confirmation, first communion, status animarum (family census) | Ages and family groups; status animarum is gold where it exists |

## Finding them
- **U.S.**: identify the parish from address, ethnicity (German "national" parishes in St. Louis were separate from territorial ones) and date. Archdiocese archives hold many older registers. Parishes may answer by mail. **Contacting a parish or archive needs the user's approval.** FamilySearch has some U.S. Catholic films.
- **Germany/Austria/Poland, etc.**: Matricula (data.matricula-online.eu, free images, Catholic dioceses incl. Münster, Osnabrück, Paderborn, Passau). FamilySearch has films (some viewable only at a FamilySearch center). Diocesan archives (Bistumsarchiv) hold the rest.
- The parish of the village: look up the place in Meyers Gazetteer (meyersgaz.org) to find its Catholic parish ("kath. Kirche" / "KPfarr").

## Latin reading aid
| Latin | Meaning |
|---|---|
| natus/nata, baptizatus/a, renatus | born, baptized |
| filius/filia legitimus/a (fil. leg.) | legitimate son/daughter |
| illegitimus, spurius | illegitimate |
| pater, mater, parentes, conjuges | father, mother, parents, married couple |
| patrinus/matrina, patrini, levans | godfather/godmother, sponsors |
| copulati sunt, matrimonium contraxerunt | were married |
| testes | witnesses |
| obiit, defunctus/a, sepultus/a | died, deceased, buried |
| viduus/vidua, relicta | widower/widow, widow of |
| coloni, agricola, sutor, faber | farmers, farmer, shoemaker, smith |
| die, mensis, anno; hora | on the day, month, year; hour |
| nata (in a woman's name) | née |
| proclamationes | banns |
Months are often abbreviated with Roman-style numerals: 7bris = September, 8bris = October, 9bris = November, Xbris = December. Source: FamilySearch Wiki "Latin Genealogical Word List".

## Reading carefully
- Transcribe exactly, mark doubtful letters "(?)", and save the image. Ask for a second reading from the user before a doubtful entry becomes a fact.
- Sponsors with the same surname as a parent suggest a sibling. Log them as a lead, not a fact.
- In German registers, the entry may be in German Kurrent script (see german-records).

## Filing
`tools/file_record.py --category church-records ...` with the register, parish, diocese, entry number, page and image URL. Mark the image reading "unverified" until checked.

skills.name: immigration-naturalization
skills.description: Use when tracing when and how an ancestor arrived in the U.S. (passenger lists, ports) or became a citizen (declarations, petitions, certificates).
skills.content:
---
name: immigration-naturalization
description: >-
  Use when tracing when and how an ancestor arrived in the U.S. (passenger
  lists, ports) or became a citizen (declarations, petitions, certificates).
---
# Immigration and naturalization

## Start from U.S. records that give the arrival year
In order: 1900/1910/1920 census (immigration year, Na/Pa/Al), naturalization papers, obituary, passport application, WWI draft card (1917-18), church records. Get a year range and a likely port before you search the lists.

## Passenger lists
| Period | What exists |
|---|---|
| 1820-1891 | U.S. Customs passenger lists (name, age, sex, occupation, country). Usually no hometown. |
| 1855-1890 New York | Castle Garden (castlegarden.org index; images on FamilySearch/Ancestry) |
| 1892-1924+ New York | Ellis Island (statueofliberty.org, free with registration. **Registration needs user approval.** Or use the FamilySearch index.) |
| From 1893 | Immigration manifests that give the last residence, a relative left behind, and who they joined in the U.S. From 1907 the place of birth is also given. |
| New Orleans, Baltimore, Galveston, Philadelphia | Major ports for Midwest-bound Germans. New Orleans then riverboat up the Mississippi was a common route to St. Louis before the railroads. |
| Departure lists | **Hamburg** lists 1850-1934 survive (Staatsarchiv Hamburg; indexed on Ancestry/FamilySearch). **Bremen** lists were mostly destroyed (only 1920-1939 fragments survive), so use U.S. arrival lists instead. |
Sources: NARA "Immigration Records" (archives.gov/research/immigration); FamilySearch Wiki "United States Emigration and Immigration"; Staatsarchiv Bremen passenger-list notes.

Published indexes: *Germans to America* (Glazier & Filby, 1850-1897) are derivative and contain errors, so always find the image.

## Naturalization
- **Before 27 Sep 1906**: any court (county, circuit, federal) could naturalize. Steps: Declaration of Intention ("first papers", any time after arrival), then a Petition/final papers after 5 years' residence, then the oath and a certificate. Pre-1906 papers are often thin (name, country, date), but the court and date still matter. Look in county circuit court records (state archives, FamilySearch films) and federal district court records (NARA).
- **1906 onward**: standardized federal forms with birth date and place, arrival ship and date, spouse and children. Duplicates are held by USCIS (USCIS Genealogy Program charges a fee, so **ask the user before any request**). Certificate files (C-files) and A-files are at NARA for older cases.
- **Derivative citizenship**: before 22 Sep 1922 (Cable Act), a wife generally became a citizen through her husband. Before 1940, minor children did so through a naturalized parent. So many women and children have no papers of their own.
- Homestead and voting records and the 1920 census year of naturalization can point to the court.
- Sources: NARA "Naturalization Records"; USCIS History Office "Genealogy" pages.

## Search loop
1. Build URLs: `tools/ftcheck.py urls "Given Surname" --born YYYY` and add variant spellings (German names were often anglicized: Gerhard→Gerard/George, Heinrich→Henry, Johann→John).
2. Search arrivals ±3 years from the census year, filtering by age.
3. Match on age, occupation, travelling companions (family groups) and destination. One match criterion is not enough: two or more independent ones are needed before it becomes a fact.
4. Once you have a hometown, switch to german-records or catholic-parish-registers.

## Filing
One source per list page or per naturalization document (`tools/file_record.py --category immigration`). Cite the ship, port, arrival date, list line and NARA microfilm series if given.

skills.name: german-records
skills.description: Use when researching an ancestor from Germany: finding the village, church books and civil registration, reading Kurrent script, and German naming customs.
skills.content:
---
name: german-records
description: >-
  Use when researching an ancestor from Germany: finding the village, church
  books and civil registration, reading Kurrent script, and German naming
  customs.
---
# German records

## 1. Pin the exact place first
You need the village, not "Germany" or "Prussia". U.S. sources that may name it: church marriage/baptism entries, naturalization (1906+), passenger manifests (1893+, birthplace 1907+), obituaries in German-language newspapers, tombstones, letters.
- Look the place up in **Meyers Gazetteer** (meyersgaz.org, the 1912 gazetteer). It gives the district (Kreis), civil registry (Standesamt) and Catholic/Protestant parishes. Many villages share a name: confirm it with nearby places named in the records.
- Borders and names changed (1871, 1919, 1945). Record the place as it was named at the time **and** its modern name and state.

## 2. Which records, which years
| Record | Coverage | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Church books (Kirchenbücher) | Often from the 1600s; many gaps from the Thirty Years' War | Catholic: Matricula (free) and diocesan archives. Protestant: Archion (paid; **needs user approval**). FamilySearch films. |
| Civil registration (Standesamt) | Prussia from 1 Oct 1874; all of the German Empire from 1 Jan 1876 (earlier in the Rhineland and other French-ruled areas, ~1798-1815+) | Local Standesamt or state/municipal archives. Online for some regions (Ancestry, FamilySearch, state archive portals). Access limits apply: births 110 years, marriages 80, deaths 30. |
| Ortsfamilienbücher (OFB, village family books) | Compiled genealogies of whole parishes | online-ofb.de and printed books (derivative: verify against the register) |
| Emigration records | Patchy (permits, newspaper notices) | State archives; regional emigrant databases |
| Military, tax, land (Hofakten) | Varies | State archives (Landesarchiv) |
Source: FamilySearch Wiki "Germany Civil Registration" and "Germany Church Records". Civil-access limits per the Personenstandsgesetz (2009).

## 3. Reading old script
- Most records before about 1900-1940 are in **Kurrent**, or Sütterlin (1915-1941). Catholic registers are often in Latin (see catholic-parish-registers).
- Use an alphabet chart (FamilySearch "German Script Tutorial", BYU script tutorial). Typical traps: e/n, h with a long descender, long ſ (s), and u marked with a hook ˘ to tell it from n.
- Transcribe letter by letter, mark doubts "(?)", and save the image. Readings stay "unverified" until a second reader (the user or another record) agrees.

## 4. Naming customs that cause false matches
- Several given names, used by the **call name (Rufname)**, often the last or middle one ("Gerhard Heinrich" may appear as Heinrich or Henry). Many siblings may share the first name "Johann" or "Maria".
- In northwest Germany (Westphalia, Emsland, Oldenburg, Osnabrück), **farm names**: a man who married onto or inherited a farm could take the farm's name ("Schulte genannt Meyer", "gen."/"vulgo"). The surname can change between records.
- Women: records often use the maiden name throughout life, or "geb." (née).
- Low German vs. standard spellings vary (Meyer/Meier/Maier, Schröder/Schroeder/Schrader). Use `tools/ftcheck.py variants`.

## 5. Contacting archives
Many German archives answer email research requests (sometimes for a fee). **Never write to or pay an archive without the user's approval for that exact request.** Draft the request (in German and English) for the user instead.

skills.name: citation-format
skills.description: Use when writing or fixing a source entry in sources.md or a SOUR record in tree.ged, so every citation is complete, consistent and lets someone find the record again.
skills.content:
---
name: citation-format
description: >-
  Use when writing or fixing a source entry in sources.md or a SOUR record in
  tree.ged, so every citation is complete, consistent and lets someone find the
  record again.
---
# Citation format (simplified Evidence Explained style)

## Rule
Every fact cites one source ID (S#). Each S# has **one line in sources.md** and **one `0 @S#@ SOUR` record in tree.ged**. `tools/file_record.py` writes both. Check that they match with `python3 tools/ftcheck.py sync`.

## sources.md line layout
`- S#: <Title>. <Repository/where + URL>. Date: <event or record date>. File: <media path>. People: <RF ids>. <What it says (key extract)>. <LEAD (unverified)> (filed YYYY-MM-DD ...)`
- **Title** (it becomes the GEDCOM TITL): record type, the person or household, place, date. Example: `1900 US census, Smith household, Ward 5, ED 12, sheet 3A`.
- **Where**: database or archive, collection name, film/item number and the URL (the image URL if possible). Add "accessed YYYY-MM-DD".
- **What it says**: the exact wording of the key facts, in quotes where read from the image, with uncertain readings marked "(?)".
- Keep it on one line, and put "Source:" detail in the note, not new lines.

## Templates by record type
| Type | Title | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Census | `YYYY US census, <Head> household, <township/ward>, <county>, <state>, ED <n>, sheet <n><A/B>, line <n>` | NARA series (e.g., T623 roll 123), FamilySearch/Ancestry URL |
| Death certificate | `Death certificate no. <n>, <Name>, <county>, <state>, <date>` | Missouri Digital Heritage, Death Certificates database, URL |
| Marriage | `Marriage license/return, <Groom> and <Bride>, <county>, <date>` | County Recorder, book/page, index or image URL |
| Church register | `<Baptism/Marriage/Burial> register, <parish>, <place>, <year>, entry <n>` | Diocese/archive, Matricula or FamilySearch film, page and URL |
| Obituary | `Obituary, <Name>, <newspaper>, <date>, p. <n>` | Newspaper archive or Legacy URL |
| Grave | `Find a Grave memorial <id>, <Name>, <cemetery>` | URL. This is a derivative record (the photo of the stone is better evidence than the transcription) |
| Passenger list | `Passenger list, <ship>, <port> arrival <date>, <Name>, line <n>` | NARA microfilm, index URL |
| Naturalization | `<Declaration/Petition> no. <n>, <Name>, <court>, <date>` | Court/NARA/FamilySearch film and URL |
| Family knowledge | `<User>, family knowledge, chat, YYYY-MM-DD h:mm AM CT: <topic>` | Chat transcript (private) |
| Online tree | `<Site> tree "<name>" (owner), <person>, accessed <date>` | URL. Always "hint only, not evidence" |

## In tree.ged
- Under each fact: `2 SOUR @S#@`, with an optional `3 PAGE <entry/line>` for the exact spot.
- Do not create a SOUR record by hand. Use `python3 tools/gedsour.py S#` to copy an existing sources.md line into tree.ged (it backs up the tree first).
- Never renumber S# ids. If two entries turn out to be the same record, keep both and note "same as S#".

## Quality check
Can a stranger find this exact page again from the citation alone? If not, add the film/roll, page, line or URL.

skills.name: conflict-resolution
skills.description: Use when two or more records disagree about a person's name, date, place or relationship, or when deciding whether a record belongs to the same person.
skills.content:
---
name: conflict-resolution
description: >-
  Use when two or more records disagree about a person's name, date, place or
  relationship, or when deciding whether a record belongs to the same person.
---
# Resolving conflicting evidence

Based on the Genealogical Proof Standard (Board for Certification of Genealogists, bcgcertification.org) and the evidence-analysis terms in Mills, *Evidence Explained*.

## 1. Classify every piece of evidence before weighing it
| Ask | Options |
|---|---|
| Source | **Original** (first recording, e.g., register image) / **derivative** (index, transcription, abstract, online tree) / **authored** (biography, compiled genealogy) |
| Information | **Primary** (informant present at the event: a parent at a baptism) / **secondary** (heard about it: a child giving a parent's birthplace on a death certificate) / undetermined (unknown census informant) |
| Evidence | **Direct** (answers the question outright) / **indirect** (must be combined with other facts) / **negative** (an absence that tells something) |
Rough weight: original + primary + made close to the event beats derivative or secondary or made decades later. Online trees and published indexes are hints, never proof.

## 2. Steps
1. **State the question exactly**: "When was X born?" not "Who is X?"
2. **List every record** that answers it, with S#, what it says, who the informant was, how long after the event it was made, and the classification above.
3. **Look for an explanation** of each disagreement: age rounding, the informant's distance from the event, transcription or indexing errors, name anglicization, calendar or place-boundary changes, two different people of the same name.
4. **Check identity first**: before treating a record as conflicting, prove that it's the same person (2+ matching independent details: spouse, parents, place, occupation, associates). Same-name neighbors are the most common error. Put a ruled-out namesake under "Ruled out" in the person note.
5. **Decide**: pick the best-supported value and give the reason in one or two sentences. If the evidence is even, record a range ("abt. 1857, 1856-1858") and keep the question open in todo.md.
6. **Record it**:
   - In the person note under **Conflicts**: `<fact>: S12 says X (primary, 1880) vs S30 says Y (secondary, 1945). Likelier X, because ...`
   - In tree.ged: the chosen value, cited to its sources. The alternate value goes in a `NOTE` with its S# (or a second event with `2 TYPE alternate`), never deleted.
   - Never present the decision as more certain than it is. Use "probable" or "possible" wording.
7. **Report to the user**: the conflict, the choice, the reason, and what record would settle it.

## Common patterns
- Census ages drifting a few years: prefer baptism or birth record > earliest census > death certificate.
- Death-certificate parents' names wrong or missing: the informant (often a child or a hospital) is secondary.
- Immigration year varying across censuses: prefer the passenger list, then naturalization papers, then the earliest census.
- Tombstone dates: made later, sometimes much later. Check the burial register or the death record.
- Family memory vs. a record: keep both. Family stories are often right about the core and wrong about details.

skills.name: gedcom-import-merge
skills.description: Use when the user supplies a GEDCOM export (Ancestry, MyHeritage, FamilySearch, Gramps) to import, compare or merge into the master tree.ged.
skills.content:
---
name: gedcom-import-merge
description: >-
  Use when the user supplies a GEDCOM export (Ancestry, MyHeritage,
  FamilySearch, Gramps) to import, compare or merge into the master tree.ged.
---
# GEDCOM import and merge

## Principles
- tree.ged is the master copy. An imported file is a **source** (a user or online tree = hint only), not a replacement.
- Never overwrite tree.ged with an export. Merge person by person, and every merged fact keeps its citation.
- Never upload tree.ged anywhere or sync it to a site without the user's approval. Living people stay private.

## Steps
1. **Save the export** as `imports/<site>-YYYY-MM-DD.ged`. Do not edit it afterwards.
2. **Back up the master**: `cp -p tree.ged backups/tree-$(date +%Y-%m-%d-%H%M)-pre-import.ged`.
3. **Check both files**:
   `python3 tools/ftcheck.py check imports/<file>.ged` and `python3 tools/ftcheck.py check tree.ged`
   Note counts of people, families and sources, missing dates, dangling links, and possible duplicates.
4. **Log the export as a source**: add one S# in sources.md (title: `<Site> tree export "<tree name>", <owner>, YYYY-MM-DD (user tree, hint only)`). Then `python3 tools/gedsour.py S#`. If the export carries its own source records (e.g., "FamilySearch Family Tree", "WikiTree"), log each as its own S#.
5. **Match people** between the export and the master:
   - Strong match: the same Soundex surname + given name or initial + birth year ±2 + at least one matching relative (spouse, parent or child).
   - Possible match: the name and dates match but no relative does. Put it in a review list and ask the user or check a record.
   - New person: no match. Only add them if they connect to someone already in the tree.
6. **Write a differences report** (`imports/<file>-differences.md`): one row per fact where the export and the master disagree or the export adds something. Columns: person, fact, master value (S#), export value, action proposed.
7. **Apply only what's supported**: facts the export adds become "unverified" NOTEs citing the export S# until a record confirms them. Conflicts go through conflict-resolution. Never replace a record-backed value with a tree-only value.
8. **Re-run the ID and index tools** if people were added (see the README: `assign_ids.py --write --csv ids.csv && build_index.py`). Then run `ftcheck check`, `ftcheck sync` and `ftcheck todo`. The goal is 0 dangling source links and 0 family links to missing people.
9. **Report**: people added and matched, facts proposed, conflicts found, and the new todo items.

## Exporting for the user
If the user wants a file to load elsewhere, copy tree.ged to an export file, remove or mark living people (keep their names only, or drop them), and hand it to the user. They do the upload.

## Common GEDCOM problems
- Custom tags (`_APID`, `_MTTAG`, `_UID`) come from the site and are safe to keep or drop. Don't treat them as evidence.
- Dates like "ABT 1850", "BEF", "AFT", "BET 1850 AND 1852" are valid GEDCOM. Keep the qualifier.
- Character encoding: export as UTF-8. Watch for umlauts turned into "Ã¼" (re-read the file as UTF-8 or latin-1).
- Long text lines continue on `CONC` (no space added) or `CONT` (new line) lines.
- Media paths in an export point at the site's server. Download the images separately only if the user wants them.

skills.name: illinois-vital-records
skills.description: Use when looking for an Illinois (including Chicago and Cook County) birth, death, marriage or divorce record, or deciding which office or database holds it.
skills.content:
---
name: illinois-vital-records
description: >-
  Use when looking for an Illinois (including Chicago and Cook County) birth,
  death, marriage or divorce record, or deciding which office or database holds
  it.
---
# Illinois vital records

Verify exact years and fees on the official sites before relying on them.

## What exists where
| Record | Years | Where | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Statewide death index | 1916-1950 (plus a pre-1916 index) | Illinois State Archives online databases (Secretary of State) | Free index with county and certificate number; order the certificate from the county clerk. |
| Statewide marriage index | 1763-1900 | Same databases | Free. Later marriages are at the county clerk. |
| Birth and death registration | Statewide from 1916; county from 1877-78 | County clerk of the event's county | Births restricted for decades; genealogical copies cost a fee. **Ask the user before ordering.** |
| Cook County (Chicago) | From 1871-72 (the 1871 fire destroyed most earlier records) | Cook County Clerk genealogy portal | Index free, copies paid. |
| Divorce, probate, early naturalization | Varies | Circuit clerk; Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) | **Contacting needs the user's approval.** |
| Church records | Often earlier | Parish or diocesan archives | See catholic-parish-registers. |
Sources: Illinois State Archives databases page; FamilySearch Wiki "Illinois Vital Records" and "Cook County, Illinois Genealogy".

## Search tips
- Pin the county first; families near St. Louis crossed the river often (also check missouri-vital-records).
- Use spelling variants and a blank first name with a narrow date range.
- FamilySearch free indexes ("Illinois, Cook County Deaths", "Illinois, County Marriages"), then find the image.
- Obituaries via library newspaper databases, Legacy.com and funeral homes; Find a Grave and Catholic cemetery offices for burials.

## Reading critically
Death facts on a certificate are primary; birth details and parents are secondary (informant). Compare with census and church records; use conflict-resolution.

## Filing
Use the filing script; cite index name, certificate or license number, county, date and URL (see citation-format).

## Never
Order a copy or write to an office or archive without the user's approval for that exact request. Living people stay private.

skills.name: greek-records
skills.description: Use when researching an ancestor from Greece or a Greek community: finding the village, Greek church and civil records, Greek naming and surname customs, shortened American surnames, and reading Greek script.
skills.content:
---
name: greek-records
description: >-
  Use when researching an ancestor from Greece or a Greek community: finding the
  village, Greek church and civil records, Greek naming and surname customs,
  shortened American surnames, and reading Greek script.
---
# Greek records

Verify archive holdings and access rules before relying on them.

## 1. Find the village first
- U.S. sources: passenger manifests (1893+; birthplace 1907+), naturalization (1906+), draft cards, U.S. Greek Orthodox parish records, obituaries, tombstones (often in Greek), letters.
- Record the place as named then **and** its modern municipality; local government was reorganized (e.g., 1997, 2011) and many villages were renamed.

## 2. Records
| Record | Gives | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Dimotologio (municipal family register) | Families with birth years | Town hall; requests usually by a relative, in Greek |
| Mitroo Arrenon (male register) | Males, birth year, father | Town hall or General State Archives (GAK) branch |
| Lixiarchio (civil registry) | Births, marriages, deaths, generally 1920s-30s on | Local civil registry |
| Orthodox church registers | Baptisms, marriages, burials | Parish, metropolis, or GAK branch |
| Electoral, school, military records | Men's ages, fathers, villages | GAK branches |
| U.S. Greek Orthodox records | U.S. sacraments | Parish or Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America archives |
Sources: FamilySearch Wiki "Greece Genealogy"; General State Archives (gak.gr). Check FamilySearch's catalog by place.

Regional notes: the Ionian Islands were Venetian then British until 1864 (older records may be Italian), and the 1953 Ionian earthquake destroyed many records. Crete, Macedonia and other areas joined Greece later, so earlier records may be in Ottoman-era archives.

## 3. Names
- First son usually named for the paternal grandfather, first daughter for the paternal grandmother, then maternal grandparents. A lead, not proof.
- Surname endings hint at region: -akis (Crete), -poulos (Peloponnese), -atos (Ionian), -idis (Pontus/Asia Minor), -oglou (Asia Minor).
- Women use the genitive surname (Papadopoulos becomes Papadopoulou; Pappas becomes Pappa) and keep the maiden name in records.
- Americanized names: surnames shortened or respelled; given names changed (Panagiotis to Peter, Konstantinos to Gus, Dimitrios to James, Vasiliki to Bessie). Search all forms and Greek script.
- Transliteration varies (Giorgos/Yiorgos/Georgios).

## 4. Reading Greek script
Use an alphabet chart and FamilySearch Greek word lists. Older records may be in katharevousa and Julian dates (Greece adopted the Gregorian calendar in 1923; add 12-13 days). Mark doubts "(?)"; readings stay unverified until checked.

## 5. Contacting offices
Never write to or pay an office without the user's approval for that exact request; draft it in Greek and English for the user.

## Filing
One source per register page or document with the filing script; cite register, municipality, archive, entry and URL (see citation-format).

skills.name: us-military-records
skills.description: Use when researching an ancestor's U.S. military service: draft cards, service and personnel files, muster rolls, unit or ship histories, pensions, discharges and veterans' burials.
skills.content:
---
name: us-military-records
description: >-
  Use when researching an ancestor's U.S. military service: draft cards, service
  and personnel files, muster rolls, unit or ship histories, pensions,
  discharges and veterans' burials.
---
# U.S. military records

Verify current rules and fees on archives.gov.

## Start with family papers
Discharge papers (DD-214, WD AGO forms), photos (insignia, rank), medals, letters, obituaries, VA markers. Note branch, war, rank and unit first.

## Records
| Record | Coverage | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Draft cards | WWI 1917-18; WWII 1940-47 incl. the 1942 "old man's" registration (born ~1877-1897) | FamilySearch (free), Fold3/Ancestry, NARA |
| Personnel files (OMPF) | 20th century | National Personnel Records Center, St. Louis, via SF-180 or eVetRecs. Archival (open) 62 years after separation; newer limited to veteran or next of kin. **Needs the user's approval and signature.** |
| 1973 NPRC fire | Destroyed ~80% of Army records 1912-1960 and ~75% of Air Force 1947-1964 (Hubbard to Z) | Navy, Marine and Coast Guard not affected; burned files rebuilt from pay vouchers, VA files, morning reports |
| Navy muster rolls | 1939-1949 | NARA; Fold3/Ancestry (user session, read-only) |
| Army morning reports, unit histories | WWII | NARA, NPRC |
| Ship histories | Navy ships | Dictionary of American Naval Fighting Ships (history.navy.mil) |
| Civil War and earlier service and pensions | Pre-1916 | NARA; indexes on FamilySearch/Fold3 |
| Burials, headstones | VA cemeteries, government stones | VA Gravesite Locator; headstone applications 1925-1963 |
| BIRLS | Veterans with a VA file | FamilySearch/Ancestry; enlistment and release dates |
| State records | Varies | State archives; discharges recorded at county recorders |
Sources: NARA "Military Records" and "The 1973 Fire"; VA Gravesite Locator; Naval History and Heritage Command.

## Search loop
1. Confirm branch and war.
2. Find the draft card.
3. Check BIRLS and the Gravesite Locator.
4. Find the unit or ship (muster rolls, morning reports, discharge).
5. Read the unit or ship history.
6. For the full file, draft an SF-180 for the user to sign and send.

## Reading critically
Service numbers and ratings (e.g., F1 = Fireman First Class) tell same-name veterans apart. Family memory of a ship is a lead until a record confirms it.

## Filing
One source per document with the filing script; cite collection, NARA series or roll, page and URL (see citation-format). Keep living veterans' details private.

## Never
Submit an SF-180, order records or sign up for paid sites without the user's approval for that exact step.
